titles.341: Annotatio I §.IV cont: Picherellus — Tertullian’s quasi vere; Origen, Augustine, Cyril on figurative eating
titles.342: Annotatio I §.IV (2): Reformed doctors — Est as significat (Zwingli) or Est signum (Oecolampadius)
titles.343: Annotatio I §.IV: Do not confuse proposition-propriety with real supernatural presence and manducation
titles.344: Annotatio I §.IV (3): Many Lutherans concede tropic speech — Marbachius vs Pezelius
titles.345: Annotatio I §.IV: Synecdoche Grammar vs Rhetoric; Mansfeld’s Calvinian vs Lutheran metonymy
titles.346: Annotatio I §.IV close IMPLICITE Pontificii: Double trope under the species — stop before Lutheran IMPLICITE

latin.341: Hujus Verba recitare operae pretium duco, tùm quòd Opuscula viri in paucorum admodum manibus versantur, tùm quòd tantò majorem fidem meretur Autor, quantò Pontificii communiter proprietatem verborum Christi pressius urgere consuevere: Cum diceret Christus Joh. 6., inquit Picherellus, nisi carnem filii hominis manducaveritis &c. intelligit Tertullianus lib. de resurrect. carnis, num. marg. 28. non verè (i. e. improprie) dixisse edendam carnem suam, durum inquit & intolerabilem existimaverunt sermonem ejus, quasi verè carnem suam illis edendam determinasset. Voces hae quasi verè, faciunt ut Tertullianus intellexerit non verè. Cui adstipulatur Origenes in Lev. cap. 7timum, qui citatur de consecr. dist. 2 can. de hac. De hac hostia, quae in Christi commemorationem mirabiliter fit, edere licet: de illa verò, quam Christus in ara crucis obtulit, secundum se edere non licet. Ad eumque modum, quia videtur hoc dicto Christus facinus vel flagitium jubere, Augustinus ait figuratam esse locutionem, de doctr. Christ. lib. 3. cap. 16. & de fide contra Manich. cap. 37. 38. & figuratam etiam agnoscit Cyrillus in libro 7timo ad Leviticum.
latin.342: (2.) REFORMATI DOCTORES ad unum omnes, qui τὸ Est, in propositione Christi, Hoc est corpus meum, vel cum Zwinglio, per τὸ significat, vel cum Oecolampadio, per τὸ Est signum seu figura corporis mei, interpretantur.
latin.343: Ad quas tamen Reformatorum doctorum Interpretationes propositionis Eucharisticae, oppidò annotandum est: Non confundendam hic quaestionem de proprietate vel improprietate propositionis Christi Eucharisticae, cum quaestione, sive de praesentia, sive de manducatione corporis Christi, in Coena, reali ac substantiali: neque enim ex negata Priori, i. e. ex negata proprietate verborum, rectè infertur posterioris negatio i. e. negatio praesentiae & manducationis realis. Prior negatio verba spectat & terminos, seu propositionem ex verbis & terminis confiatam; posterior rem ipsam hujusque attributa. Prior, formaliter accepta, Logica magis, posterior verò magis Metaphysica. Propositio Christi: Hoc, i. e. hic panis est corpus meum, potest esse impropria, etiamsi corpus Christi, quod impropriè de pane hoc loco praedicatur, propriè, i. e. reverâ in Eucharistia & praesens sit & manducetur, supernaturali scilicet & spirituali nobisque imperceptibili modo. Sicuti enim, non per solam propositionis Christi assertam proprietatem, corpus ejus in Coena supernaturali modo praesens asseritur reque ipsâ manducari, ita nec per solam propositionis ejusdem negatam proprietatem, corpus ejus supernaturali modo vel praesens, vel re ipsâ manducari negatur. Praesentia pariter ac manducatio corporis Christi supernaturales & spirituales, eaeque quàm maximè reales & substantiales, (unicum illum à Christo definitum praesentiae & manducationis corporis sui, tàm intra, quàm extra Eucharistiam, modum designantes) ex cap. 6. Johan. & 1. Cor. 10. satis superque intelliguntur & citra omnem controversiam admittuntur, etiamsi propositio Institutionis S. Coenae definitiva: Hoc est corpus meum, ad modum definitivarum Sacramentalium omnium, impropria seu figurata ac tropica defendatur.
latin.344: (3.) LUTHERANI NON PAUCI, partim eorum, qui tropicam in genere, eorum partim, qui vel Metonymicam, vel Synechdochicam in specie, concedunt. Ex prioribus memoramus Marbachium contra Pezelium, p. 36. disertis verbis passum, in propositione: Hoc est corpus meum, non in universum omnem figuratam locutionem excludi, sed eam tantùm, quae à propria singularum vocum significatione nos cogit deflectere; In qua Marbachii determinatione facilè acquieverint Reformati, tropicam duntaxat locutionem urgentes, modum ejus non ita, sed promiscuè potiùs habentes, tropus ne in verbis, vel in praedicatione, collocetur.
latin.345: Ex posterioribus, quà Synechdochen, praeter Selneccerum ipsumque Lutherum, innumeri alii, cum distinctione tamen inter Synechdochen Grammaticam & Rhetoricam, cujus Distinctionis applicatione ad praesentem materiam, quantum in Grammaticam peccetur, vel illi norunt, qui nondum aere lavantur. Nam ubi quaeso traditur in Grammaticis Synecdoche, pro quali contendunt Theologi hi? Quanquam Synecdoche, sive Grammatica dicatur, sive alio veniat nomine, tropus tamen ac figura remanet, juxta ac metonymia, metaphora aut ironia: Id quod docet tropi natura, nominis dissimulatione haud tollenda nec mutanda, cùm ipsa re obtinetur. Quà Metonymiam autem, Mansrafius in Erotematibus ad articulos quatuor Visitatorios, non minus in propositione definitiva partis prioris Sacrae Coenae, quàm posterioris ista: Hoc poculum, est N. T. in sanguine meo, metonymiam largiturus, sed sub distinctione satis ridicula inter Metonymiam Calvinianam de signo & signato, & Metonymiam Lutheranam, quâ uti effectus pro causa ponitur, in hac propositione: Poculum est Testamentum in sanguine meo, i. e. sanguis in poculo est illud quo sancitum est N. T., id est promissio remissionis peccatorum; ita Continens pro contento in hac: Hic panis est Corpus meum.
latin.346: IMPLICITE vero tropicam efficiunt propositionem quicunque hactenus aliter quam Reformati, eam interpretati sunt, tam Pontificii, quàm Lutherani, utrique tamen explicitè pro proprietate verborum, tanquam pro aris & focis, dimicantes. PONTIFICII propositionem: Hoc est corpus meum, interpretati per hanc: Id quod continetur sub speciebus panis & vini, est corpus meum, duplicem tropum ei inesse disertè ostendunt, primò Synechdochen, quum hoc (quod demonstrat substantiam cum accidentibus) ad accidentia propriè pertinere statuitur; deinde Metonymiam Continentis pro Contento. Taceo, dicentem, Propositionem, Hoc est corpus meum, tantundem significare, quantum, sub hisce speciebus seu accidentibus est corpus meum, re ipsâ negare verba illa propriè & ut sonant, accipienda, suâque ἐκθέσει hypothesin subvertere. Assertionis ratio solida est, quia hoc modo pervertitur (1) Subjecti & Attributi sedes: nam corpus meum fit Subjectum, & Hoc, Attributum. Deinde, sensus vocis, Hoc, falso & indoctè permutatur verbis istis, sub Hoc, vel sub hisce speciebus i. e. accidentibus, quae toto categoriae genere differunt, Gomar. loc. cit. p. 142. num. 63. 64.

pass_a.341: I judge it worth the work to recite this man’s words, both because the man’s Opuscula are in very few hands, and because the Author deserves so much the greater faith the more the Pontificians commonly press the propriety of Christ’s words more closely: When Christ said in John 6, says Picherellus, Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man &c., Tertullian (On the Resurrection of the Flesh, marg. no. 28) understands that He said His flesh was to be eaten not truly (i.e. improperly) — they judged His speech hard and intolerable, as if He had truly determined His flesh to be eaten by them. These words as if truly make Tertullian to have understood not truly. To whom Origen on Leviticus ch. 7 agrees (cited de consecr. dist. 2 can. de hac): Of this host which is wonderfully made in Christ’s commemoration it is lawful to eat; but of that which Christ offered on the altar of the cross it is not lawful to eat according to itself. And to that mode, because by this saying Christ seems to command a crime or outrage, Augustine says the locution is figurative (On Christian Doctrine bk. 3 ch. 16; On Faith against the Manichees ch. 37–38); and Cyril also acknowledges it figurative in book 7 on Leviticus.
pass_a.342: (2.) The REFORMED DOCTORS to a man, who interpret the Est in Christ’s proposition This is my body either with Zwingli by significat, or with Oecolampadius by Est the sign or figure of my body.
pass_a.343: Yet to those Interpretations of the Reformers’ doctors of the Eucharistic proposition it is especially to be annotated: The question of the propriety or impropriety of Christ’s Eucharistic proposition is not here to be confused with the question either of the presence or of the manducation of Christ’s body in the Supper, real and substantial: nor from the denied Prior — i.e. from denied propriety of the words — is the negation of the posterior rightly inferred, i.e. negation of real presence and manducation. The prior negation regards words and terms, or the proposition composed of words and terms; the posterior the thing itself and its attributes. The prior, taken formally, is more Logical; the posterior more Metaphysical. Christ’s proposition This, i.e. this bread is my body, can be improper, even if Christ’s body, which is here improperly predicated of the bread, is properly — i.e. in truth — both present in the Eucharist and eaten, namely in a supernatural and spiritual mode imperceptible to us. For just as not by the asserted propriety of Christ’s proposition alone is His body asserted present in the Supper in a supernatural mode and eaten in the very thing, so neither by the denied propriety of the same proposition alone is His body denied present or eaten in the very thing in a supernatural mode. The supernatural and spiritual presence and manducation of Christ’s body — and those most highly real and substantial (designating that unique mode of presence and manducation of His body defined by Christ, both within and outside the Eucharist) — are understood more than enough from John 6 and 1 Cor. 10 and admitted without all controversy, even if the definitive Institution proposition This is my body is defended as improper or figurative and tropical after the manner of all definitive Sacramentals.
pass_a.344: (3.) NOT A FEW LUTHERANS — partly of those who concede the tropic in genus, partly of those who concede either the Metonymic or the Synechdochic in species. From the former we mention Marbachius against Pezelius, p. 36, expressly having allowed that in the proposition This is my body not every figurative locution absolutely is excluded, but only that which forces us to deflect from the proper signification of the several vocables; In which determination of Marbachius the Reformed will easily have rested, urging only tropic locution, not so much its mode, but rather holding promiscuously whether the trope is placed in the words or in the predication.
pass_a.345: From the latter, as to Synecdoche, besides Selneccer and Luther himself, innumerable others — yet with a distinction between Grammatical and Rhetorical Synecdoche, by whose application to the present matter how much is sinned against Grammar even those know who are not yet washed with bronze. For where, I ask, is Synecdoche handed down in the Grammars for such as these Theologians contend? Although Synecdoche, whether called Grammatical or coming under another name, remains nonetheless a trope and figure, just as metonymy, metaphor, or irony: Which the nature of a trope teaches, not to be removed or changed by dissimulation of the name when the thing itself is obtained. But as to Metonymy, Mansfeld in Erotemata on the four Visitatorial articles, about to grant metonymy no less in the definitive proposition of the prior part of the Sacred Supper than of the posterior This cup is the N.T. in my blood — yet under a distinction ridiculous enough between Calvinian Metonymy of sign and thing signified, and Lutheran Metonymy by which as effect is put for cause in this proposition The Cup is the Testament in my blood, i.e. the blood in the cup is that by which the N.T. is ratified, that is the promise of remission of sins; so Containing for contained in this: This bread is my Body.
pass_a.346: But IMPLICITE whoever hitherto have interpreted that proposition otherwise than the Reformed make it tropical — both Pontificians and Lutherans — both sides nonetheless fighting explicitly for the propriety of the words as for hearths and altars. The PONTIFICIANS, having interpreted This is my body by this: That which is contained under the species of bread and wine is my body, expressly show a double trope in it — first Synecdoche, when this (which demonstrates substance with accidents) is determined to belong properly to the accidents; then Metonymy of Container for Contained. I pass over in silence one saying that the Proposition This is my body signifies as much as under these species or accidents is my body — in the very thing denying those words are to be taken properly and as they sound, and by his own ἔκθεσις overthrowing the hypothesis. The solid reason of the assertion is that in this way is perverted (1) the seat of Subject and Attribute: for my body becomes the Subject, and This the Attribute. Then the sense of the voice This is falsely and unlearnedly exchanged for those words under This, or under these species i.e. accidents, which differ by a whole category genus — Gomarus loc. cit. p. 142 nos. 63–64.

341: Picherellus is worth quoting: few own his Opuscula, and a Pontifician witness carries extra weight when his own side presses Christ’s words as proper.

On John 6’s Unless you eat the flesh… he reads Tertullian as taking the eating not truly — i.e. improperly — because the hearers treated the sermon as hard as if He had truly set His flesh to be eaten (quasi vere → non vere).
Origen, Augustine, and Cyril likewise mark figurative speech for that hard saying.
342: (2.) The Reformed doctors as one interpret the Est in This is my body either with Zwingli as significat, or with Oecolampadius as Est the sign or figure of my body.
343: Do not mix the propriety of Christ’s Eucharistic proposition with the question of real substantial presence and manducation in the Supper.
Deny propriety of the words, and you still have not denied real presence or eating — the first fight is logical (words/terms); the second metaphysical (the thing).

This bread is my body can be improper while Christ’s body is truly present and eaten supernaturally and spiritually (John 6; 1 Cor. 10) — just as asserting propriety alone does not prove that presence.
344: (3.) Not a few Lutherans concede tropic speech in genus, or metonymy / synecdoche in species.
Marbachius against Pezelius allows that This is my body does not shut out every figure — only the kind that forces us off each word’s proper signification.
On that the Reformed easily rest, pressing tropic locution while caring less whether the trope sits in the words or in the predication.
345: On synecdoche, Selneccer, Luther, and countless others distinguish Grammatical from Rhetorical synecdoche — a distinction that sins against Grammar for anyone not still wet behind the ears.
Call it Grammatical or not: synecdoche remains a trope, like metonymy, metaphor, or irony.

Mansfeld grants metonymy in both halves of the Institution, yet under a rather ridiculous split between Calvinian sign/thing-signified metonymy and Lutheran effect-for-cause / container-for-content metonymy.
346: IMPLICITE, whoever interprets the proposition otherwise than the Reformed also make it tropical — Pontificians and Lutherans alike — even while both fight explicitly for word-propriety as for hearth and altar.
The Pontificians’ That which is contained under the species of bread and wine is my body embeds a double trope: synecdoche (this → accidents) and metonymy of container for contained.

Swap This is my body for under these accidents is my body and you deny proper hearing in the act — subject and attribute seats flip, and This is falsely traded for under these species (Gomarus, p. 142).
Stop before Lutheran IMPLICITE readings (Luther’s in/cum/sub; Flacius’s duplex mass).

notes.346: IMPLICITE Pontificii double trope; stop before Lutheran IMPLICITE.

346.english: for hearths and altars / for all they hold dear
